items.title: Parents: please don’t buy Grand Theft Auto VI for your child
items.summary: Rockstar Games’ brilliant 18-rated criminal caper is stuffed with sex, drugs and violence. It is the most explicit game I’ve ever played – and it really is not for kidsI am haunted still by an interaction I had at my stepson’s ninth birthday party in 2014, where one of the kids asked if I could put on Grand Theft Auto V for them all. “I have it at home!”, he said, giving me the puppy-dog eyes. Mentally replaying that game in my head, flashing back to the many scenes involving such things as smoking meth, over-the-top gratuitous violence and grubby sex in one character’s trailer, I said “no way”. Later I gently mentioned to the kid’s mother that GTA V was an 18-rated game and really wasn’t suitable for kids. “Oh, but he’s really good at these games,” she told me. She was genuinely shocked to learn that an 18-rating on a video game was a flag for adult content, rather than an indication of its difficulty.Grand Theft Auto VI is released this week. It is an incredible creative and technical feat, conjuring a realistic-looking and exhaustively detailed virtual Florida filled with every kind of filth and criminality you could imagine. It is brilliant, entertainingly observed and even sometimes unexpectedly touching, largely thanks to a central love story between the player couple, Jason and Lucia. It is lewd, violent and frequently hilarious. It is also absolutely full of stuff that I really would not want my 10 and seven-year-old boys to see or hear. I have never played a game that has more thoroughly earned its 18 rating. Continue reading...

items.title: Danny Kelly loved football and never forgot the absurdity of earning a living talking about it | Max Rushden
items.summary: The journalist and broadcaster who died last week aged 69 knew the enduring power of radio, even as the landscape changed so quicklyIt’s injury time at the Emirates on 29 October 2008, Arsenal are 4-3 up against Tottenham. Tom Huddlestone cushions a ball to Luka Modric, whose strike takes a deflection. It loops over Manuel Almunia and off a post into the path of Aaron Lennon, who prods it home and starts skipping towards the Spurs supporters before diving on to the ground and being enveloped by Modric, Benoît Assou-Ekotto, Darren Bent and a couple of pitch-invading fans. Pandemonium, for once, seems the apt way to describe it.But the real entertainment is happening in a radio studio at 18 Hatfields, London SE1; the old home of TalkSport. As the goal goes in, a guttural voice makes an indecipherable but very loud noise. It’s hard to transcribe – perhaps “ERRRRRAAAARRRGGHH”, or maybe “OOEEERRAAGGH”. It’s just a noise, but it’s unmistakably Danny Kelly. He regains the power of speech and follows it up with: “Gooooaaaal … Goalll Stan, Goalll at the Emirates.” Reporter Ian Abrahams and Stan Collymore join the excitement, before Danny comes back: “I LOVE FOOTBALL, STAN, I LOVE IT.” It is such a brilliant piece of radio. From one of the absolute greats. Continue reading...

items.title: You have to laugh at LIV’s collapse but the saga reveals money is golf’s core value | Jonathan Liew
items.summary: Why do rich powerful men love golf? Ultimately the sport exists in a world where the politics is assumed to be settledFarewell, then, LIV Golf. As its original figurehead Greg Norman once so delicately put it, albeit in a slightly different context: we’ve all made mistakes, you learn from those mistakes, and you move forward. Forward – in LIV’s case – to bankruptcy court and the start of liquidation proceedings some time in January 2027. And not without a certain irony, in the sense that Norman’s cherished project, established over a cacophony of human rights concerns, ended up getting dismembered and terminated on the orders of the Saudi government. Life moves on you pretty fast.Perhaps the funniest part of LIV’s protracted demise – unless you count the television viewing figures – has been the last seven months, after Saudi Arabia abruptly pulled the plug on the seemingly abundant flow of money that had fuelled its astonishing rise. Suddenly LIV’s chief executive, Scott O’Neil, was forced to take his begging bowl up and down midtown Manhattan, panhandling for change, drawing up entirely conceptual revenue forecasts, pretending for all the world that this was an actual, real-life business proposition; a legitimate going concern with profits and a bottom line and a plan for the future.
